Pregnancy

Ovarian torsion during pregnancy: symptoms, scans and urgent treatment

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Ovarian torsion means that an ovary, sometimes together with its fallopian tube, twists around its supporting tissues and threatens its blood supply. During pregnancy, sudden one-sided lower abdominal pain needs urgent assessment. Prompt treatment aims to protect your health, the pregnancy and as much ovarian tissue as possible.

What twists, and why it matters

The ovaries contain eggs and produce hormones. They sit beside the uterus, supported by tissues that carry blood vessels; the nearby fallopian tubes are separate structures. Twisting can obstruct blood leaving the ovary and eventually blood entering it. Swelling and prolonged oxygen shortage can damage tissue.

A twisted ovary is different from a cyst that is simply present on a scan. Many cysts need only planned monitoring, whereas suspected torsion is an urgent surgical problem. The term adnexal torsion can include the ovary and tube; rarely the tube twists on its own.

Symptoms: do not wait for a complete pattern

Pain is often sudden and mainly on one side of the lower abdomen, with nausea or vomiting. It can come and go if twisting is intermittent. Tenderness may occur; fever is possible but is not required. Bleeding does not establish torsion and may indicate another pregnancy problem. Temporary improvement does not reliably make it safe to wait.

Get emergency help now for severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain on movement or touch, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, light-headedness or passing out, shoulder-tip pain, difficulty breathing, heavy vaginal bleeding or sudden confusion. Any one of these patterns is enough; you do not need all of them. Do not drive yourself. New one-sided pain, especially with vomiting, needs urgent in-person assessment even without these additional signs.

Cysts, ovarian stimulation and other risk factors

An enlarged ovary or a cyst can make twisting more likely. Many associated masses are benign, but their nature still needs assessment. Torsion can occur without a previously known cyst. Greater mobility of the supporting tissues may also contribute; a single cause cannot always be identified.

Pregnancy and fertility treatment involving ovarian stimulation are important contexts to tell the team about. Studies of women already selected for emergency surgery cannot tell every pregnant person her individual risk. A particular cyst diameter, age, or side of pain cannot confirm or exclude torsion; do not wait for a cyst to reach a specified size.

Why early pregnancy needs particular attention

After ovulation, the corpus luteum develops in the ovary and supplies hormones that support early pregnancy until the placenta takes over. A corpus-luteum cyst or stimulated enlarged ovaries can be part of the setting in which torsion occurs. This does not mean that normal pregnancy hormones inevitably cause twisting.

Pregnancy case series contain many first-trimester cases, but torsion also occurs later. As the uterus grows, the ovaries may change position and be harder to see. There is no safe gestational week after which new concerning pain can be dismissed, and no reliable home check based on which side hurts.

Other causes of pain must also be considered

Ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, appendicitis, kidney stones, urinary infection and bowel illness can resemble parts of the same picture. Later pregnancy brings additional possibilities, including contractions or placental problems. Ordinary nausea or ligament pain should not be assumed to explain a new severe or unusual episode.

Contact maternity or urgent pregnancy care immediately for abdominal pain with spotting or bleeding, regular cramps or tightenings, lower back pain, unusual vaginal discharge or fluid leakage, painful or newly urgent/frequent urination, or cloudy, pink, red or brown urine. Use emergency help for the severe patterns above. Tell the team your gestational age, fertility treatment, known cysts and when symptoms began.

Examination and ultrasound are the starting point

The team assesses your symptoms, pulse and other observations, abdominal findings and pregnancy. Blood or urine tests can help investigate infection, bleeding or other causes, but no single laboratory result rules torsion out. An examination or scan of the pregnancy alone does not necessarily assess both ovaries adequately.

Ultrasound through the abdomen, and sometimes a vaginal scan with consent, looks at the ovaries, nearby structures and pregnancy. Doppler assesses blood flow, but visible flow does not exclude torsion. In one retrospective pregnancy study, flow was still detected in 18 of the 48 women who had Doppler testing despite surgically confirmed torsion. This is a selected study group, not a population risk estimate.

When another scan or an operation is needed

If ultrasound leaves an important question unanswered, MRI without contrast may help assess the ovaries or another cause of pain when it is available promptly. MRI is not reserved for late pregnancy. Contrast and any other imaging require an individual benefit–risk decision; necessary diagnostic care should not be withheld solely because you are pregnant.

Scans cannot always settle the diagnosis. When suspicion remains high, the specialist may recommend an operation to inspect the ovary and treat twisting at the same time. A reassuring scan should not override concerning clinical findings, and additional imaging should not cause an unsafe delay. The consent discussion should include the possibility of a different finding at surgery.

Urgent surgery aims to preserve the ovary

The surgeon usually aims to untwist the affected structures and preserve ovarian tissue where possible. A cyst may be treated during the same operation if appropriate. A dark or swollen appearance alone is not a dependable measure of permanent ovarian damage; preservation principles in adolescent guidance need to be applied with pregnancy-specific judgment.

Sometimes removal of an ovary or tube is necessary because tissue cannot be preserved, bleeding cannot be controlled or another serious finding changes the plan. Ask what was found, what was preserved and whether tissue results need follow-up. Losing one ovary does not automatically mean infertility, although future fertility depends on the remaining ovary, tubes and other factors.

Keyhole or open surgery: an individual decision

Laparoscopy uses small abdominal incisions and is often an option during pregnancy. Open surgery may be needed according to the clinical situation, uterine size, mass, surgical access and available expertise. There is no universal rule that every early case needs laparoscopy and every later case needs an open operation. Medically necessary surgery should not be postponed to reach another trimester.

Evidence does not justify promising that either route has no fetal risk. A 2024 torsion cohort found no significant difference in measured pregnancy outcomes between routes, but the groups differed in gestational age. A 2026 review of mixed abdominal operations found an association between laparoscopy and fetal loss alongside maternal benefits; most studies were retrospective, and its adnexal-mass subgroup was inconclusive. These findings support individualized counselling, not a fixed route for every pregnancy.

Anaesthesia and pregnancy monitoring

The obstetric, surgical and anaesthetic teams balance the risks of the illness, delay and operation together. Standard anaesthetic agents have not been shown to cause human birth defects at usual clinical concentrations, but that does not guarantee every pregnancy outcome. Studies of surgery and anaesthesia are difficult to separate from the underlying illness, and some outcomes remain uncertain.

Monitoring of the pregnancy depends on gestational age, the procedure and local facilities. The team also plans pain relief, clot prevention and observation for contractions or other complications. Ask who will coordinate your pregnancy care after surgery. Concerns about anaesthesia deserve discussion, but should not lead you to decline or delay necessary emergency treatment without specialist advice.

Corpus-luteum surgery and progesterone support

If the corpus luteum or the ovary containing it must be removed early in pregnancy, the team considers whether hormone support is needed before placental production is established. The older SAGES guideline specifically discusses progesterone after corpus-luteum removal before 12 weeks. This is a clinician-managed decision based on the actual operation and pregnancy stage.

It is not a rule that everyone with pain, a cyst or detorsion needs progesterone. Do not start, stop or change a fertility-clinic prescription yourself, and do not copy a dose from an online case report. Before discharge, confirm whether support is needed, the prescribed plan, its review or stopping point and whom to contact if doses are missed or symptoms recur.

Possible complications and recovery

Untreated or delayed torsion can damage the ovary and, in severe cases, lead to tissue death, infection or inflammation inside the abdomen. Maternal illness and the episode of surgery may threaten the pregnancy. These are reasons for prompt care, not a prediction that ovarian loss, miscarriage or infertility is inevitable.

After treatment, follow the individual wound, activity, medicine and pregnancy follow-up plan. Confirm any cyst or tissue-result review and whether another scan is needed. New or returning concerning pain needs reassessment even after successful untwisting; do not assume it is ordinary recovery. Emergency symptoms remain emergencies after discharge, while fever, persistent vomiting or a wound concern also warrant prompt contact with the treating team.

Questions that help you understand the plan

Useful questions include: How strongly is torsion suspected? Have both ovaries and other urgent causes been assessed? What would another scan change? Why is this operation and route recommended now? Can ovarian tissue be preserved, and might the corpus luteum be affected? Asking should support consent without delaying urgent care.

Record your symptom timeline, medicines, fertility procedures and known scan findings if you can do so without delaying assessment. After treatment, ask for the operative findings, pregnancy-monitoring plan, any hormone instructions and a clear contact route. Research can explain choices, but a study average cannot predict your own outcome.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Seek urgent assessment for new concerning pain; bring the symptom timeline and fertility or cyst information if readily available.

Before discharge, confirm operative findings, pregnancy follow-up, any prescribed hormone plan and the route for urgent help.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organize symptoms, existing scan findings and questions about surgery, pregnancy monitoring and medicines. It cannot diagnose torsion, judge ovarian viability, select an operation or replace emergency care.

When to seek help

Get emergency help for severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain on movement or touch, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, light-headedness or passing out, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion. Any one pattern is enough; do not drive yourself. New one-sided pain needs urgent assessment even if it eases or a previous Doppler showed flow.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • New one-sided pain in pregnancy needs prompt assessment; severe or other emergency patterns need immediate help.
  • Pain may come and go, and Doppler blood flow may remain visible despite torsion.
  • Pregnancy, enlarged ovaries and fertility treatment matter, but no cyst-size threshold safely excludes torsion.
  • Necessary surgery should not wait for another trimester; ovarian preservation and the surgical route are individualized.
  • Early corpus-luteum removal may require prescribed hormone support; never self-prescribe or change it.

Frequently asked questions

Is ovarian torsion dangerous during pregnancy?

Yes. Impaired blood supply can damage the ovary and serious illness can threaten the pregnancy. Prompt assessment and treatment aim to reduce those risks. It does not mean that pregnancy loss or removal of the ovary is inevitable.

Which symptoms require emergency help?

Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain on movement or touch, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, light-headedness or passing out, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion needs emergency help. Do not wait for all signs and do not drive yourself. New one-sided pain with vomiting also needs urgent assessment.

What usually makes an ovary twist?

An enlarged ovary or cyst may increase the tendency to twist around its supports; ovarian stimulation and pregnancy are relevant contexts. It can also happen without a known cyst. Neither the side nor a particular cyst diameter is a reliable home diagnostic rule.

Can the pain stop and the Doppler scan look normal?

Yes. Symptoms can be intermittent and blood flow may remain visible. Neither finding safely excludes torsion when the clinical picture is concerning. Return for urgent assessment if symptoms persist or recur.

Does surgery have to wait until the second trimester?

No. Medically necessary treatment should not be delayed to reach a preferred trimester. The team selects laparoscopy or open surgery according to your condition, pregnancy stage and operative circumstances; neither route comes with a universal no-risk guarantee.

Will the ovary always be removed?

No. Untwisting and preserving ovarian tissue is an important goal when feasible. Removal may still be necessary for specific operative findings. Appearance alone does not reliably establish permanent damage; ask what was found and what was preserved.

Will I need progesterone after treatment?

Possibly, particularly if the corpus luteum is removed early, before placental hormone production is established. Your team decides from the pregnancy stage and procedure. It is not required automatically after every episode, and you should not choose or change a dose yourself.

Can the pregnancy continue after torsion surgery?

Many reported pregnancies have continued after treatment, but studies cannot guarantee an individual outcome. Disease severity, pregnancy stage and other factors matter. Follow the pregnancy and surgical plans, and seek reassessment for returning pain or new warning symptoms.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
